passages.title: The Downstate Campaign
passages.text:
In 1963, a three-week-long demonstration for jobs at the construction site of the Downstate Medical Center in Brooklyn, New York, became one of the most significant and widely publicized campaigns of the civil rights movement in the United States. An interdenominational group made up mostly of locally based African American ministers, who had remained politically moderate until then, organized and led hundreds of people in an aggressive protest. Their efforts relied mainly on the participation and direct financial support of the ministers’ own congregations and other congregations throughout Brooklyn. The goal of this campaign was to build a mass movement that would force changes in government policies as well as in trade union hiring practices, both of which they believed excluded African Americans from construction jobs.

Inspired by the emergence of African American religious leaders as key figures elsewhere in the civil rights movement, and reasoning that the ministers would be able to mobilize large numbers of people from their congregations and network effectively with other religious leaders throughout the city, the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), a national civil rights organization, had decided to ask the ministers to lead the Downstate campaign. However, by organizing a civil disobedience campaign, the ministers were jeopardizing one of the very factors that had led CORE to seek their involvement: their positions as politically moderate community leaders. Urban African American ministers and churches had been working for decades with community and government organizations to address the social, political, and economic concerns of their communities, and ministers of African American congregations in Brooklyn had often acted as mediators between their communities and the government. Many of them also worked for major political parties and ran for political office themselves. By endorsing and leading the Downstate protest, the ministers were risking their political careers and their reputations within their communities for effecting change through established political channels.

The Downstate campaign ended with an agreement between the ministers and both government and union officials. This agreement did not include new legislation or a commitment to a specific numerical increase in jobs for African Americans, as the protestors had demanded. But even though some civil rights activists therefore considered the agreement incomplete, government officials did pledge to enforce existing antidiscrimination legislation. Moreover, the Downstate campaign effectively aroused public concern for the previously neglected problem of discrimination in the construction industry. It also drew public attention, which had hitherto focused on the progress of the civil rights movement primarily in the southern United States, to the additional need to alleviate discrimination in the North. Finally, throughout the campaign, the ministers managed to maintain their moderate political ties. The dual role played by the ministers—activists who nonetheless continued to work through established political channels—served as a model for future ministers who sought to initiate protest actions on behalf of their communities.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The 1963 Downstate Medical Center protest in Brooklyn led by African American ministers and its impact on the civil rights movement.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy (with a touch of Problem / Solution)

**Main Point**

The Downstate Medical Center protest was a milestone civil rights action led by politically moderate African American ministers, who balanced activism with continued engagement in established political channels; this set a precedent for future civil rights leadership in northern cities.
The key "Most Valuable Sentence" encapsulating the main point appears near the end of the last paragraph: "The dual role played by the ministers—activists who nonetheless continued to work through established political channels—served as a model for future ministers who sought to initiate protest actions on behalf of their communities."

**P1: Introduction to the Downstate Protest**

This paragraph introduces the Downstate protest as an influential and widely publicized civil rights campaign in Brooklyn. It highlights the unusual leadership of locally based, previously moderate African American ministers, describes how they organized and funded the protest through their congregations, and outlines their goal of forcing changes to discriminatory government and union hiring policies.

**P2: The Ministers’ Role and the Risks They Took**

Here we learn why national civil rights organization CORE encouraged the ministers to lead the protest and how the ministers' involvement broke with their traditionally moderate, politically connected roles. The paragraph discusses the tension between their new activism and their established positions, emphasizing that by leading the protest, they risked losing political influence and community trust.

**P3: Outcomes and Broader Significance**

The final paragraph sums up the results: although the protest didn't achieve all its demands, it did secure promises to enforce existing anti-discrimination laws and brought public attention to job discrimination in the North. Critically, the ministers preserved their moderate standing while being effective activists, creating a model for future civil rights leadership.

questions.prompt: It can be reasonably inferred from the passage that the author's attitude is most favorable toward which one of the following?

choices.text: the ways in which the Downstate campaign altered the opinions of union leaders
choices.explanation:
The beginning of the final paragraph says that the Downstate campaign ended with an agreement with union officials that did **not** include new legislation or a commitment to a specific numerical increase in jobs, as demanded.

So the author probably wouldn't be most impressed by this, since it's unclear how much the opinions of union leaders were even altered.

choices.text: the impact that the Downstate campaign had on the implementation of new anti-discrimination legislation
choices.explanation: The agreement included no new legislation. Officials pledged to enforce existing antidiscrimination law. This answer refers to an impact on implementation of new legislation that the passage does not report.

choices.text: CORE’s relationship to the demonstrators in the Downstate campaign
choices.explanation: The passage describes hundreds of participants and the ministers' leadership, but does not evaluate CORE's relationship with demonstrators. Its explicit favorable assessment instead concerns the campaign effectively arousing public concern.

choices.text: the effects that the Downstate campaign had on public awareness
choices.explanation:
We can match this up with the middle of the final paragraph:

*the Downstate campaign **effectively** aroused public concern for the previously neglected problem of discrimination in the construction industry.*

choices.text: the way in which the leaders of the Downstate campaign negotiated the agreement that ended the campaign
choices.explanation:
The beginning of the final paragraph says that the Downstate campaign ended with an agreement with union officials that did **not** include new legislation or a commitment to a specific numerical increase in jobs, as demanded.

So the author probably wouldn't be most impressed by this, since the protesters didn't really get any of the big things they were asking for.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following assertions about the results of the Downstate campaign does the author affirm in the passage?

choices.text: It achieved all of its participants’ goals for changes in union policy but not all of its participants’ goals for government action.
It directly achieved neither all of its participants’ goals for government action nor all of its participants’ goals for changes in union hiring policies.
It achieved all of its participants’ goals for changes in government policies, but did not achieve all of its participants’ goals for union commitment to hiring policies.
It achieved all of its particular goals for government action immediately, but only gradually achieved some of its participants’ desired effects on public opinion.
It eventually achieved all of its participants’ particular goals for both government action and establishment of union hiring policies, but only after extended effort and significant risk.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the reference to past activities of ministers and churches (third sentence of the second paragraph) is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is a Local Purpose question (in order to / serves to / primarily to), so we expect that the correct answer will reinforce language from some *Framing Idea* that comes right **before** the detail, or, less commonly, from some *Takeaway* that comes right **after** the detail.

Right before the highlighted text, we're being told that the ministers' involvement in the Downstate campaign could jeopardize their position as politically *moderate* community leaders, which is the whole reason that CORE wanted them in the first place.

The highlighted text goes on to tell us about the activities of these ministers, which include affiliating themselves with community and government organizations to address community needs.

Right after the highlighted text, we get a reiteration of the fact that the ministers' involvement in leading the Downstate campaign was **jeopardizing / risking** their reputations as "people who effect change through established political channels", which we could read as a synonym for "Politically moderate community leaders".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The big idea the correct answer should be reinforcing is that the ministers were doing something unusual / risky / out-of-step with their normal reputation.

However the highlighted text is telling us that is was very usual and on-brand for these ministers to be trying to address social / political / economic issues. So maybe the highlighted text is telling us, "What was new / risky for these ministers wasn't the idea of getting *political* on behalf of community members, but more *the way* in which they were getting political."

They are leading a civil disobedience campaign, which is radical not moderate, which is working *outside* established political channels.

choices.text: demonstrate that the tactics used by the leaders of the Downstate campaign evolved naturally out of their previous political activities
choices.explanation: The prior activities illustrate work through established community and government channels. Leading civil disobedience introduced a different tactic and risked the ministers' moderate reputations. The passage does not present this tactical change as a natural continuation, though the underlying community goals continued.

choices.text: explain why the leaders of the Downstate campaign decided to conduct the protest in the way they did
choices.explanation:
The highlighted text talks about what the ministers had been doing in the community for the last few decades.

It doesn't offer any reason **why** they are doing something *radically different* when it comes to how they're conducting the Downstate campaign (i.e. using civil disobedience rather than working through established political channels as they've always previously done).

choices.text: provide examples of the sorts of civil rights activities that the leaders of CORE had promoted
choices.explanation: The highlighted text has nothing to do with CORE. It describes what the ministers were doing in the decades prior to when CORE reached out to talk to them.

choices.text: indicate how the Downstate campaign could have accomplished its goals by means other than those used
choices.explanation:
The author never suggests that the choice to use civil disobedience was an unnecessary one, or that the ministers could have accomplished their goals at least as well by working with community and government organizations, through established political channels.

This paragraph is telling us that for these ministers, the means used were different from the norm. This answer is telling us that the means used weren't important or crucial.

choices.text: underscore the extent to which the Downstate campaign represented a change in approach for its leaders
choices.explanation:
This reinforces the "Bookend" ideas, as we expect on Local Purpose questions. Both before and after the highlighted text, the paragraph is conveying the idea that "by doing civil disobedience, ministers were **jeopardizing/risking** their reputations and political careers", which implies that they are doing something that is at odds with their reputation / with their customary approach.

The highlighted text shows a group of ministers working in a moderate way within established political channels.

The Downstate campaign used civil disobedience, which is nothing like their previous tactics. It's sort of analogous to a middle-manager who for decades tried to improve conditions for her subordinates by having many meetings and conferences with the top brass, but then one day she decides to tell her employees that they all should go on strike.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following does the author affirm in the passage?

choices.text: CORE was one of several civil rights organizations that challenged the hiring practices of the construction industry.
The Downstate campaign relied primarily on CORE and other national civil rights organizations for most of its support.
After the Downstate campaign, concern for discrimination in the construction industry was directed primarily toward the northern United States.
Many ministers of African American congregations in Brooklyn had sought election to political office.
In response to the Downstate campaign, union officials pledged to adopt specific numerical goals for the hiring of African Americans.

questions.prompt: The passage most clearly suggests that which one of the following is true of the group of ministers who led the Downstate campaign?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What do we learn about these ministers who led the campaign? Well, a lot really.

1st paragraph:
- politically moderate until this protest
- organized / led 100's of people in an aggressive protest
- were funded by their own congregations and others in Brooklyn
- they though AA's were being excluded from construction jobs

2nd paragraph:
- by getting into civil disobedience, they were jeopardizing their reputation as moderates
- for decades, churches had worked to better their communities and these ministers had often acted as mediators between the communities and the government
- many worked for major political parties / ran for office themselves

3rd paragraph:
- they ultimately agreed to an end to the protest, in conjunction with the government and union officials
- they managed to maintain their moderate political ties
- they served as a model for future ministers to initiate protest actions on behalf of their communities.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Cool, so we know just those 374 things about these ministers. :)

We would never have time to comb the whole passage again looking for all those tidbits. If the question stem clue words (i.e. "group of ministers") is too omnipresent throughout the passage, we tend to just go right into the answer choices, filter out ones that sound crazy strong or out of scope, and research any that we think we might be able to match up with some supporting line.

choices.text: The Downstate campaign did not signal a significant change in their general political and social goals.
choices.explanation:
This is tricky because the Downstate campaign *did* signal a significant change in their ****tactics****. They went from being moderate intermediaries between community and government to being "radical" civil disobedient protesters.

But it didn't change their ****goals****.

In the middle of the 2nd paragraph, it says that, *"Urban African American ministers and churches had been working for decades with community and government organizations to address the social, political, and economic concerns of their communities".*

The goal of the Downstate campaign (end of 1st paragraph) was *"to build a mass movement that would force changes in government policies as well as in trade union hiring practices, which they felt were excluding African Americans".*

So are the political / social goals of the Downstate campaign in a similar realm to "addressing the social, political, and economic concerns of their communities?"

Sure -- trying to get jobs is definitely an economic concern. And feeling like you're being marginalized because you're African American is a social / political concern.

choices.text: After the Downstate campaign, they went on to organize various other similar campaigns.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: various other campaigns
choices.explanation: The conclusion says their dual role served as a model for future ministers. It does not report that these same leaders subsequently organized similar campaigns. Continuing established political work does not rule such campaigns out; it simply does not establish them.

choices.text: They had come together for the purpose of addressing problems in the construction industry well before CORE’s involvement in the Downstate campaign.
choices.explanation: Their earlier work addressed social, political and economic concerns generally. The passage does not specify a prior joint effort on construction-industry problems before CORE's involvement. That narrower history cannot be inferred from the general account.

choices.text: They were criticized both by CORE and by other concerned organizations for their incomplete success in the Downstate campaign.
choices.explanation: In the 3rd sentence of the last paragraph, we hear that some activists considered the agreement reached to be incomplete, but we're never told anything resembling the idea that CORE actually criticized these ministers who responded to their call for help.

choices.text: Prior to the Downstate campaign, many of them had not been directly involved in civil rights activities.
choices.explanation:
We're told that prior to this campaign, they had for decades worked to address social, political, and economic concerns of their communities, via established political channels.

We don't know for sure if those social / political / economic concerns involved civil rights activities, but we definitely are never told that it ****didn't**** involve civil rights. We have no textual ammunition to support this language that many of them had never engaged in civil rights activities before.

We're even told that "elsewhere in the civil rights movement, African American religious leaders had emerged as key figures".

passages.title: Cultural Revolution Artistic Effects
passages.text:
The Cultural Revolution of 1966 to 1976, initiated by Communist Party Chairman Mao Zedong in an attempt to reduce the influence of China’s intellectual elite on the country’s institutions, has had lasting repercussions on Chinese art. It intensified the absolutist mind-set of Maoist Revolutionary Realism, which had dictated the content and style of Chinese art even before 1966 by requiring that artists “truthfully” depict the realities of socialist life in China. Interest in nonsocial, nonpolitical subjects was strictly forbidden, and, during the Cultural Revolution, what constituted truth was entirely for revolutionary forces to decide—the only reality artists could portray was one that had been thoroughly colored and distorted by political ideology.

Ironically, the same set of requirements that constricted artistic expression during the Cultural Revolution has had the opposite effect since; many artistic movements have flourished in reaction to the monotony of Revolutionary Realism. One of these, the Scar Art movement of the 1980s, was spearheaded by a group of intellectual painters who had been trained in Maoist art schools and then exiled to rural areas during the Cultural Revolution. In exile, these painters were for perhaps the first time confronted with the harsh realities of rural poverty and misery—aspects of life in China that their Maoist mentors would probably have preferred they ignore. As a result of these experiences, they developed a radically new approach to realism. Instead of depicting the version of reality sanctioned by the government, the Scar Art painters chose to represent the “scarred reality” they had seen during their exile. Their version of realist painting emphasized the day-to-day hardships of rural life. While the principles of Revolutionary Realism had insisted that artists choose public, monumental, and universal subjects, the Scar artists chose instead to focus on the private, the mundane, and the particular; where the principles of Revolutionary Realism had demanded that they depict contemporary Chinese society as outstanding or perfect, the Scar artists chose instead to portray the bleak realities of modernization.

As the 1980s progressed, the Scar artists’ radical approach to realism became increasingly co-opted for political purposes, and as this political cast became stronger and more obvious, many artists abandoned the movement. Yet a preoccupation with rural life persisted, giving rise to a related development known as the Native Soil movement, which focused on the native landscape and embodied a growing nostalgia for the charms of peasant society in the face of modernization. Where the Scar artists had reacted to the ideological rigidity of the Cultural Revolution by emphasizing the damage inflicted by modernization, the Native Soil painters reacted instead by idealizing traditional peasant life. Unfortunately, in the end Native Soil painting was trivialized by a tendency to romanticize certain qualities of rural Chinese society in order to appeal to Western galleries and collectors.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The influence of the Cultural Revolution on Chinese art and the artistic movements that emerged in response to it.

**Framework**

Old / New

**Main Point**

The restrictive, politicized artistic rules of the Cultural Revolution initially limited artistic expression in China, but these same constraints later inspired a wave of new, more personally and socially critical styles of art, such as the Scar Art and Native Soil movements—though even these new movements faced their own limitations and commercial pressures. (The Most Valuable Sentence is the opening of paragraph 2: “Ironically, the same set of requirements that constricted artistic expression during the Cultural Revolution has had the opposite effect since; many artistic movements have flourished in reaction to the monotony of Revolutionary Realism.”)

**P1: The Cultural Revolution’s Artistic Restrictions**

We learn how the Cultural Revolution forced Chinese artists to follow strict political rules, only depicting a government-approved reality and forbidding nonpolitical or independent subjects. Art was used as a propaganda tool, with the government defining "truth."

**P2: The Rise of Scar Art—A New Kind of Realism**

Ironically, those same restrictions later sparked creative reactions. After being exiled to rural areas, artists started Scar Art in the 1980s, rejecting government-sanctioned perfection and choosing instead to represent the grim, real-life struggles of rural China. Scar Art focused on ordinary, individual experiences rather than grand, idealized scenes.

**P3: Evolution and Commercialization—Native Soil Movement**

As Scar Art became politicized, some artists moved on to the Native Soil movement, which focused more on nostalgia and celebrating traditional peasant life. However, this newer style also lost some authenticity, as it began to idealize rural China partly to attract Western art buyers.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following titles most accurately captures the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage was movements in Chinese art from 1966-1989.

Why was the author writing about this topic? What was her purpose? What framework did we use?

We probably used a *Highlight Noteworthy* framework, since the passage was pretty descriptive / reporting in nature.

What did the author seem to find interesting or important about these movements in Chinese art?

The first sentence of the passage says, "The Cultural Revolution **has had lasting repercussions** on Chinese Art". The author does talk about the Cultural Revolution both in the 2nd paragraph, while discussing Scar Art and in the 3rd while discussing Native Soil.

The transition into the 2nd paragraph has a rhetorical flourish from the author. She thinks it's interestingly ironic that the same set of requirements that intensified Revolutionary Realism during the Cultural Revolution also had the opposite effect later on.

The 3rd paragraph also connects Native Soil to the Cultural Revolution.

So let's look for a title that connects these art movements to the repercussions of the Cultural Revolution.

choices.text: “Painting and Politics: A Survey of Political Influences on Contemporary Chinese Art”
choices.tag: Only One Influence / Out of Scope: contemporary
choices.explanation: The passage traces a particular legacy of the Cultural Revolution: reactions against its restrictions and their later development. It is not a general survey of political influences on contemporary art. Revolutionary Realism already existed before the Cultural Revolution, which intensified its absolutist requirements.

choices.text: “How Two Movements in Chinese Painting Transformed the Cultural Revolution”
choices.tag: Reversed Causal Relationship / Two vs. Three Movements
choices.explanation:
This title is suggesting that we'll read an essay in which Scar Art and Native Soil transform the Cultural Revolution.

But as our *Most Valuable Sentence* (the 1st) reminds us, Scar Art and Native Soil are **repercussions** of the Cultural Revolution.

They are effects, not causes.

Also, this answer leaves out one of the 3 movements (presumably Revolutionary Realism).

choices.text: “Scarred Reality: A Look into Chinese Rural Life in the Late Twentieth Century”
choices.explanation: This title makes it seem like we'll read an article about the day to day conditions of Chinese peasants working in the fields, instead of the passage we did read about art movements.

choices.text: “The Rise of Realism in Post-Maoist Art in China”
choices.explanation:
The first two movements (Revolutionary Realism and Scar Art) both purported to be realist, although in very different ways.

However, the third movement, Native Soil "**idealized** traditional peasant life .. romanticizing certain qualities of rural Chinese society". It was not about gritty realism. It was about appealing to Western collectors who wanted a portrait of non-miserable Chinese farmers.

It's also not correct to call Revolutionary Realism a **post**-Mao art movement. It seems like that movement began before and continued through the Cultural Revolution instigated by Mao.

choices.text: “The Unforeseen Artistic Legacy of China’s Cultural Revolution”
choices.explanation: The opening identifies lasting repercussions of the Cultural Revolution, and paragraph 2 describes the ironic flourishing of movements reacting against the restrictions. Scar Art and Native Soil exemplify that unforeseen legacy. Revolutionary Realism supplies the restrictive background; it was not itself created afterward as part of that legacy.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following works of art would be most compatible with the goals and interests of Scar Art as described in the passage?

choices.text: a painting of a village scene in which peasants commemorate a triumph over cruel political officials
a painting symbolically representing the destruction caused by a large fire
a painting depicting the weary face of a poorly clothed peasant toiling in a grain mill
a painting caricaturing Mao Zedong as an overseer of farm workers
a painting of two traditionally dressed peasant children walking in a summer wheat field

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements about realism in Chinese art can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

choices.text: The artists who became leaders of the Native Soil movement practiced a modified form of realism in reaction against the styles and techniques of Scar Art.
Chinese art has encompassed conflicting conceptions of realism derived from contrasting political and artistic purposes.
The goals of realism in Chinese art have been effectively furthered by both the Scar Art movement and the Native Soil movement.
Until the development of the Scar Art movement, interest in rural life had been absent from the types of art that prevailed among Chinese realist painters.
Unlike the art that was predominant during the Cultural Revolution, Scar Art was not a type of realist art.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be LEAST likely to agree with which one of the following statements regarding the Cultural Revolution?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
When it comes to the Main Point, we should have internalized that the author thinks that the Cultural Revolution (in pushing artists to make art that glamorized contemporary Chinese government and society) had the ironic effect of spurring the "rebellious" Scar Art and Native Soil art movements.

We can find more details about the Cultural Revolution throughout the 1st and 2nd paragraph, so if we want to remind ourselves of other buzzphrases, we have stuff like:
- absolutist mind-set
- truth was determined by the government's preferences
- art was supposed to depict social, political subjects (pubic, monumental, and universal subjects) and show off how great everything was

It's unclear with these LEAST LIKELY questions whether we'll be eliminating four things we can support and picking one that is more irrelevant, or whether we'll be eliminating four irrelevant answers and picking one that nearly contradicts the passage.

LEAST LIKELY MOST LIKELY
contradicts < unsupported < supported

choices.text: It had the ironic effect of catalyzing art movements at odds with its policies.
choices.explanation: This is supported by the 1st sentence of the 2nd paragraph.

choices.text: The art that was endorsed by its policies was less varied and interesting than Chinese art since the Cultural Revolution.
choices.explanation:
The art that was endorsed by the policies of the Cultural Revolution was Revolutionary Realism.

The 1st sentence of the 2nd paragraph says that "many artistic movements have flourished in reaction to the **monotony** of Revolutionary Realism".

choices.text: Much of the art that it endorsed did not accurately depict the realities of life in China but rather a politically motivated idealization.
choices.explanation:
The art that was endorsed by the policies of the Cultural Revolution was Revolutionary Realism.

Did the author think that Revolutionary Realism depicted a politically motivated idealization?

For sure, in the 2nd paragraph the author said that it depicted "the version of reality sanctioned by the government", whereas Scar Art "confronted the harsh realities of rural poverty and misery that the Maoists preferred to ignore."

choices.text: Its effects demonstrate that restrictive policies generally foster artistic growth more than liberal policies do.
choices.explanation: The author describes an ironic reaction to particular restrictions: movements flourished against the monotony they imposed. This does not establish the general comparative claim that restrictive policies foster growth more than liberal policies. The passage offers no such comparison and emphasizes the restrictions' original constricting effect.

choices.text: Its impact has continued to be felt in the Chinese art world years after it ended.
choices.explanation: This is supported by the 1st sentence of the passage, which says that the Cultural Revolution has had lasting repercussions on Chinese art.

questions.prompt: The primary function of the first paragraph is to

choices.text: introduce the set of political and artistic ideas that spurred the development of two artistic movements described in the subsequent paragraphs
acknowledge the inescapable melding of political ideas and artistic styles in China
explain the transformation of Chinese society that came about as a result of the Cultural Revolution
present a hypothesis about realism in Chinese art that is refuted by the ensuing discussion of two artistic movements
show that the political realism practiced by the movements discussed in the ensuing paragraphs originated during the Cultural Revolution

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following views of the Native Soil movement?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Native Soil was discussed in the final paragraph. Do we see any lines that seem to feature the author's voice?

She says a causal claim
- "a preoccupation with rural life gave rise to Native Soil"

A description of the style
- "focused on native landscape and embodied a growing nostalgia for the charms of peasant society in the face of modernization"

A connection between Native Soil + Cultural Revolution
- Native Soil reacted to the ideological rigidity of the Cultural Revolution by idealizing traditional peasant life.

Critical reception of Native Soil
- trivialized for its tendency to romanticize certain aspects of rural Chinese society in order to pander towards Western art buyers.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: We have a handful of options, so let's look for any answer we can support using one or more of these.

choices.text: Its development was the inevitable consequence of the Scar Art movement’s increasing politicization.
choices.explanation:
The author does think that there was a backlash to the increasing politicization of Scar Art, which led many to abandon it.

But she doesn't announce any causal connection as strong as "Native Soil was an ****unavoidable / inevitable / foregone conclusion**** once Scar Art starting getting more political."

She actually identifies the main impetus of Native Soil as "a preoccupation with rural life", not a disgust with Scar Art's politicization.

choices.text: It failed to earn the wide recognition that Scar Art had achieved.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: Scar Art's wide renown
choices.explanation:
This makes an unsupported comparison about how widely recognized Scar Art vs. Native Soil was.

The passage never gives us any way to compare how widely they were recognized. We have no information about how popular Scar Art was / wasn't with the general population. Just because Native Soil ended up being trivialized doesn't mean it didn't earn at least as wide recognition as Scar Art had when it first came onto the scene.

choices.text: The rural scenes it depicted were appealing to most people in China.
choices.explanation:
We have no idea to what extent the majority of people in China liked or disliked Native Soil.

The only sentiment we have that approaches information regarding how well it was / wasn't received is actually a negative one in the final sentence.

choices.text: Ironically, it had several key elements in common with Revolutionary Realism, in opposition to which it originally developed.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: several things in common
choices.explanation: Both movements involve idealization, but the passage does not identify several shared key elements. It instead contrasts Revolutionary Realism's politically sanctioned image of contemporary society with Native Soil's nostalgic traditional peasant life. One noted similarity does not establish the broader comparison.

choices.text: Its nostalgic representation of rural life was the means by which it stood in opposition to Revolutionary Realism.
choices.explanation:
We can match this to a line in our Support Window, the second to last sentence of the passage:

*the Native Soil painters reacted to the ideological rigidity of the Cultural Revolution by idealizing traditional peasant life*

How do we know that "reacted to" should be thought of as "in opposition to"? If we go back to the beginning of the 2nd paragraph, it sets up the framing idea for the rest of the passage:

*many artistic movements have flourished in reaction to the monotony of Revolutionary Realism*

Again, it's saying "reacting to" not "opposition to", but the word ****monotony**** is negative. Reacting to a negative is generally to oppose that negative thing.

Similarly, in the second to last line of the passage, it says they're reacting to the ****rigidity****, which is also a negative word.

passages.title: Family Dispute Resolution
passages.text:
Individual family members have been assisted in resolving disputes arising from divorce or separation, property division, or financial arrangements, through court-connected family mediation programs, which differ significantly from court adjudication. When courts use their authority to resolve disputes by adjudicating matters in litigation, judges’ decisions are binding, subject only to appeal. Formal rules govern the procedure followed, and the hearings are generally open to the public. In contrast, family mediation is usually conducted in private, the process is less formal, and mediators do not make binding decisions. Mediators help disputing parties arrive at a solution themselves through communication and cooperation by facilitating the process of negotiation that leads to agreement by the parties.

Supporters of court adjudication in resolving family disputes claim that it has numerous advantages over family mediation, and there is some validity to this claim. Judges’ decisions, they argue, explicate and interpret the broader social values involved in family disputes, and family mediation can neglect those values. Advocates of court adjudication also argue that since the dynamics of power in disputes are not always well understood, mediation, which is based on the notion of relatively equal parties, would be inappropriate in many situations. The court system, on the other hand, attempts to protect those at a disadvantage because of imbalances in bargaining power. Family mediation does not guarantee the full protection of an individual’s rights, whereas a goal of the court system is to ensure that lawyers can secure all that the law promises to their clients. Family mediation also does not provide a formal record of the facts and principles that influence the settlement of a dispute, so if a party to a mediated agreement subsequently seeks modification of the judgment, the task of reconstructing the mediation process is especially difficult. Finally, mediated settlements divert cases from judicial consideration, thus eliminating the opportunity for such cases to refine the law through the ongoing development of legal precedent.

But in the final analysis, family mediation is better suited to the unique needs of family law than is the traditional court system. Proponents of family mediation point out that it constitutes a more efficient and less damaging process than litigation. By working together in the mediation process, family members can enhance their personal autonomy and reduce government intervention, develop skills to resolve future disputes, and create a spirit of cooperation that can lead to greater compliance with their agreement. The family mediation process can assist in resolving emotional as well as legal issues and thus may reduce stress in the long term. Studies of family mediation programs in several countries report that the majority of participants reach a full or partial agreement and express positive feelings about the process, perceiving it to be more rational and humane than the court system.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Family mediation vs. court adjudication for resolving family disputes

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

While there are valid arguments in favor of court adjudication in family disputes, family mediation, in the end, is better suited to the unique needs of family law because it promotes cooperation, efficiency, personal autonomy, and emotional healing. (Most Valuable Sentence: P3, first sentence: "But in the final analysis, family mediation is better suited to the unique needs of family law than is the traditional court system.")

**P1: Differences Between Mediation and Court Adjudication**

This paragraph introduces the two main ways families can resolve disputes: traditional court litigation and family mediation. It contrasts them: courts are formal, public, and binding, while mediation is more private, informal, and the mediator simply helps the parties reach their own agreement.

**P2: Arguments for Court Adjudication**

Here, the supporters of court adjudication get their say. They argue that the court process upholds social values, protects people with less power, aims to protect legal rights, creates a public/legal record, and helps to refine the law. The paragraph lists a bunch of drawbacks of mediation compared to the court process.

**P3: Arguments for and Endorsement of Family Mediation**

This paragraph pivots to the author's own take: mediation is ultimately a better fit for family law issues. The author (and mediation proponents) point out mediation is more efficient, less stressful, encourages cooperation, helps people learn skills for future disagreements, and can encourage greater compliance. Plus, real-world studies say people find mediation more rational and humane than court.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Recent studies show that family mediation is preferred by family members for resolving family disputes because it is more rational and humane than the court adjudication process.

Even though a majority of participants in family mediation programs are satisfied with the settlements they reach, the use of court adjudication in resolving family disputes has several advantages over the use of mediation.
When given the option, family members involved in disputes have typically elected to use family mediation rather than court adjudication to settle their disputes.

While court adjudication of family disputes has certain advantages, family mediation serves the needs of family members better because it enhances autonomy and encourages greater communication and cooperation in reaching an agreement.

Although supporters of court adjudication argue that family mediation does not contribute to the development and refinement of legal precedent, they fail to recognize that most family disputes can be resolved without appeal to legal precedents.

choices.text: to illustrate that court adjudication can have certain benefits that family mediation may lack
to present material that reveals the inherent limitations of the court adjudication model
to prove that the assumptions implicit in court adjudication and family mediation are irreconcilable
to present an alternative judicial option that combines the benefits of both court adjudication and family mediation
to suggest that lawyers are essential for the protection of individual rights during disputes

choices.text: A labor relations specialist assists a group of auto assembly workers and the plant’s management in reaching an agreeable salary increase for the workers.

choices.text: is more time-consuming than court adjudication
almost always results in full agreement among the parties
